History of Present Illness

History of Present Illness
Information on when the bump was noted, associated symptoms, and changes in size or
appearance can be documented. A history of rapid growth may increase suspicion for
malignancy; however, malignancies are rare in this region and they may be slow-
growing. Most bumps cause little or no pain. People often misperceive the bump as the
source of arm pain.
Medical History

Medical History
Inquire about any prior history of malignancy, renal pathology, thyroid or parathyroid
disease, or family history of similar lesions1-4 (Resources 1, 2, 3, and 4).
Physical Examination
The physical examination of a tumor in the hand and wrist includes assessment and
documentation of the following:
Size
Color changes
Borders
Tenderness
Neurovascular status
Paresthesias with percussion (Tinel sign)
Movement with adjacent musculotendinous structures
Pulsatile
Texture
Transillumination


Physical Examination
The size, color changes, location, and consistency of a mass are documented. This helps
formulate the differential diagnosis and facilitate serial comparisons. Determine if a
mass is associated with or affects regional musculotendinous or neurovascular
structures. The presence of tenderness on palpation or the presence of a pulsatile
nature of the lesion may help direct subsequent workup. Most masses encountered are
not tender or painful. Clarifying this may relieve some anxiety and correct an important
and common misconception before deciding on management. Surgeons should evaluate
the neurovascular status of both upper extremities to allow for side-to-side
comparison.1,3.4
Imaging Studies
Radiography in two or three planes
CT
MRI with and without contrast
Ultrasonography
Bone scintigraphy

Imaging Studies
Imaging studies are not necessary for most masses. If warranted, radiographs may
suffice. For radiographic lesions that have lytic areas, blastic regions, cortical disruption,
or are poorly defined, additional imaging studies may be helpful. Although not routinely
necessary, advanced imaging studies may better define size, location, and structural
characteristics for atypical lesions. For example, CT may be considered for bony or
calcifying lesions, MRI for deep or poorly defined soft-tissue masses, or ultrasonography
for cystic or vascular presentations. This additional information may provide information
that may be helpful in counseling patients to consider observation or surgical
treatment.3,4

Surgical Planning
Needle biopsy or aspiration: cystic lesions
Core needle biopsy: larger lesions (>2 to 4 cm)
Excisional biopsy: smaller (<2 to 4 cm) or larger benign lesions confirmed via physical
examination/imaging studies
Surgical management: must adhere to oncological principles

Surgical Planning
For the common, classically presenting benign mass, evidence shows that submitting a
specimen to pathology for a diagnosis that is easily confirmed during surgical
management (eg, ganglion cyst) may not be beneficial. If in doubt, send the specimen. If
any concern for malignancy exists, it often is appropriate for the surgeon who will be
performing the definitive treatment to perform the biopsy. Improperly performed biopsy
may alter the treatment plan and affect patient prognosis. The arm can be elevated
before inflation of the tourniquet rather than exsanguinated with the use of an elastic
bandage because of a theoretic risk of propagating tumor cells.
A longitudinal incision along the anticipated limb salvage approach through a single
compartment should be used to avoid seeding additional compartments with tumor
cells. Take care with hemostasis. Although not routinely necessary, surgeons should
consider acquiring cultures in patients with questionable or unclear diagnoses. In the
rare scenario of a high suspicion for malignancy and with access to an experienced
musculoskeletal pathologist, a frozen section may be viewed. This may allow for
definitive diagnosis and simultaneous definitive surgical management. Otherwise, if the
definitive diagnosis is in question, definitive surgical management should be staged until
a permanent section is reviewed.1,3-5

Classification
A benign tumor or tumor-like condition in the latent stage remains stable in appearance
or may spontaneously resolve. Therefore, observation is a treatment option. A bump in
the active stage grows, but remains confined to anatomic barriers. Locally aggressive
tumors grow and expand beyond anatomic borders extending into adjacent structural
compartments.1,3,4

Epidemiology and Pathology
Second most common benign soft-tissue tumor of the hand
Giant cell tumor of tendon sheath is histologically similar to pigmented villonodular synovitis.
Currently, both typically are called tenosynovial giant cell tumor.
Diagnosis
Nontender slow-growing firm mass, usually in the finger
More commonly located in radial three digits
Radiographs of some long-standing tumors may demonstrate associated loss of adjacent
bone.
Management
Surgical excision
Low recurrence with complete resection

Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor
Tenosynovial giant cell tumor is one of the most common soft-tissue lesions of the hand
and wrist. Because of its histological appearance, giant cell tumor of tendon sheath
currently is conceptualized as part of the disease continuum of pigmented villonodular
synovitis.6 Histologic examination will reveal proliferating villous synovitis that may be
stained deep brown secondary to hemosiderin deposition. Photomicrographs will reveal
sheets of round to ovoid mononuclear cells and osteoclast-like giant cells with thin
bands of collagen stroma. They are most commonly found around the distal
interphalangeal (DIP) joints of the radial three digits in adult patients in their 40s or 50s.

Patients typically present with a painless, long-standing, firm soft-tissue mass, which may
be multilobular. Surgical excision must include removal of any tumor extension into the
adjacent joint or tendon sheath. The risk for recurrence is low if complete excision is
performed. Factors associated with recurrence include incomplete resection, location at
the DIP joint, evidence of adjacent bone erosion, or adjacent degenerative joint disease.7
Fibroma of Tendon Sheath
Incidence
Uncommon compared with giant cell tumor of tendon sheath
Histology and Gross Appearance
Histologically, spindle-shaped fibroblasts in stroma of dense collagenous matrix with few to no
giant or xanthoma cells
Gross appearance usually is a pale or tan/gray well-circumscribed lesion.
Diagnosis
Small defined tumor attached to digital tendon sheath
Usually involves thumb
Management
Excision: surgical excision generally is curative.

Fibroma of Tendon Sheath
Macroscopically, fibromas of tendon sheath present in a similar manner to tenosynovial
giant cell tumors; however, they tend not to have the same degree of hemosiderin
pigmentation. Histologically, they tend to have a uniform appearance of haphazardly
arranged fibroblasts in a stroma of dense collagenous matrix and few to no giant cells.
For most patients, simple marginal excision is curative with low risk for recurrence.1

Lipoma
Etiology
Lipomas in the hand and wrist have similar features to other parts of the body and appear as
mature adipose tissue on histology.
Diagnosis
On physical examination, lipomas appear as soft, nontender masses, often with indistinct
borders.
May transilluminate
On MRI, lipomas appear as homogenous, well-circumscribed masses with similar signal to
normal fat.
Management
Marginal excision typically is adequate if necessary.
Low recurrence can be expected after surgical excision.

Lipoma
Lipomas in the hand and wrist present in a similar fashion to those in other parts of the
body as a slow-growing, painless mass. Imaging studies may not be routinely necessary
for patients who present with a classic history and physical examination. If a patient
reports a history of rapid growth or well-defined pain, surgeons should include
liposarcoma or angiolipoma in the differential diagnosis. Lipoma also can grow over
time, particularly if the patient also has gained weight. If in doubt, the appearance on
MRI often is diagnostic as a well-defined mass with similar homogenous signal to normal
fat on T1-weighted and T2-weighted images. In comparison, liposarcomas have
increased heterogeneity and lack of suppression on fat-suppressed MRIs. Small lipomas
may be observed. With a classic presentation, marginal excision is considered
appropriate for definitive surgical management without the need for staged biopsy or
frozen section. Studies report low risk for recurrence or malignant transformation.1,5

Hemangioma
Etiology
Hemangiomas are a proliferation of blood vessels.
They often appear during infancy.
Hemangiomas exist in two main phases
Proliferating
Involuting
Late presenting hemangiomas rarely spontaneously resolve.
Diagnosis
On physical examination, they often present as a red or bluish appearing mass.
Occasionally, they may present in a fashion similar to venous malformations.
Occasionally, secondary bleeding, ulceration, infections, or coagulopathy (Kasabach-Merritt
syndrome) may occur.
MRI with contrast often is beneficial for diagnosis.
Management
Observation may often be recommended for most patients as the natural history often is self-
limiting.
50% of hemangiomas involute by age 5 years
70% of hemangiomas involute by age 7 years
Resection may be considered if persistently symptomatic
The recurrent rate is low after surgical excision.

Hemangioma
Hemangiomas are benign soft-tissue tumors that result from the uncontrolled
proliferation of blood vessels. The timing of presentation affects prognosis. If present in
infancy, the natural history for most is for involution by age 7 years. Therefore,
observation and supportive care, such as NSAIDs or a gentle compressive dressing, are
the recommended approach if patients are minimally symptomatic. The main indications
for formal management of infantile hemangiomas is if the tumor results in ulcerations or

cardiopulmonary function. Oral propanolol is considered a first-line treatment option
and an alternative to surgical management in this setting. It has been reported to lead to
rapid shrinkage of infantile hemangioma with a minimum of 6 months of management.
Although the risk for side effects with beta-blockers are reportedly low at recommended
doses, patients should be closely monitored for adverse effects if this approach is used.
If hemangioma persists into later childhood, the likelihood of self-resolution is
considered low. Patients typically present with a red or blue-tinged soft-tissue mass. At
times, they may ulcerate, bleed, clot, or develop a secondary infection. MRI with contrast
or angiography may help confirm the diagnosis. MRI with contrast will reveal increased
signal on T1-weighted and T2-weighted images with numerous small blood vessels and
fatty infiltration. Focal areas of low signal on MRI with contrast are signs of blood flow or
calcifications. Consideration may be given to serial embolization for local control;
however, surgical resection often is curative for symptomatic lesions.1,3

Located in the dermal retinacular layer of skin or subungual
Diagnosis
Bluish-red subungual lesion
Exquisitely pinpoint painful
Cold hypersensitivity of fingertip
MRI often is helpful to support the diagnosis and for preoperative localization.
Management
Surgical resection


Glomus
A glomus body is a normal anatomic structure with a composition includes perivascular
smooth muscle cells that regulate blood flow and temperature. Proliferative growth of a
modified version of these perivascular smooth muscle cells may lead to the benign
glomus tumor.
The glomus tumor typically presents under and around the nail bed; however, they may
exist in any location. Patients usually present with pinpoint pain and cold intolerance of
the involved digit. Close examination will reveal a bluish-red lesion.
Surgical excision typically is curative with low recurrence. Surgical management of
subungual lesions involves removal of a portion or all the nail plate followed by a
longitudinal incision in the nail bed. The tumor often can be readily identified and
separated from normal surrounding soft tissue. After removal, the nail bed is repaired or
grafted and a dressing is placed.1,8

Etiology
Proliferation of Schwann cells in peripheral nerve
Nuclei of cells have palisading arrangement (Verocay bodies)
Diagnosis
Typically, painless, slow-growing well-circumscribed mass adherent to a peripheral nerve
Occasionally, secondary neurologic symptoms from mass effect
Positive Tinel sign
Characteristic appearance on MRI with or without contrast
Biopsy may damage the nerve and is avoided for typical lesions.
Management


Schwannoma
A schwannoma results from unrestrained growth of Schwann cells. On histology, distinct
hypercellular areas (Antoni A) and hypocellular (Antoni B) areas are present. The nuclei
of the involved cells are peripherally located perpendicular to the surface and parallel to
each other (ie, palisading arrangement).
Most schwannomas are painless; however, they occasionally may result in neurologic
symptoms secondary to compression of adjacent nerve fibers. On MRI, schwannomas
typically are positioned eccentrically within the nerve. Intraoperatively, a schwannoma
typically is well-circumscribed and can be separated from traversing nerve fascicles via
microscopic technique.1,8

Arise from connective tissue of peripheral nerve sheath
Neurofibroma contains mainly fibroblasts but also nonmyelinating Schwann cells, perineural
cells, and mucoid.
Diagnosis
Typically, painless, slow-growing well-circumscribed mass adherent to a peripheral nerve
May develop with cutaneous lesions
Occasionally, secondary neurologic symptoms from mass effect
Positive Tinel sign
MRI with or without contrast
Biopsy
May be associated with neurofibromatosis


Neurofibroma
Neurofibroma results from unrestrained growth of connective tissue of the peripheral
nerve sheath, particularly the endoneurium. They typically occur sporadically but may be
associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 (von Recklinghausen disease). On histology,
surgeons will discover hypocellular stroma with wire-like collagen fibers. The cellular
component is mostly fibroblasts but also may contain perineural cells, Schwann cells,
mast cells, lymphocytes, and mucoid material.
Neurofibromas, on MRI are classically positioned central to the nerve fibers. In patients
with neurofibromatosis type 1, neurofibromas fall into one of four distinct variants:
cutaneous lesions, localized intraneural tumors, plexiform neurofibromas, and massive
soft-tissue neurofibromas. Most cases involve cutaneous nerves. They can be intimately
associated with major nerve fascicles (ie, plexiform subtype) making it difficult to always
separate the two. If a neurofibroma involves a major nerve, end-to-end or nerve grafting
typically is required after tumor resection. Malignant transformation is rare and is more
of a concern in patients with neurofibromatosis (10% to 15% risk).1,8

Extraosseous Chondroma/Synovial Chondromatosis
Extraosseous chondroma or synovial chondromatosis are growth of mature lobulated
hyaline cartilage within soft tissue. Radiographs often reveal dense calcification lesion.
Patients present with a gradually enlarging soft-tissue mass that may be painful,
particularly if within the synovium. Imaging studies often are diagnostic. If symptomatic,
successful management can be achieved via open surgical excision for extra-articular
lesions or arthroscopic débridement for limited intra-articular lesions. Recurrence rates
are reportedly low if complete excision is performed.1
Leiomyoma
Etiology
Smooth muscle cells
Diagnosis
Well-circumscribed, painless mass
Vascular leiomyoma may develop calcifications and become painful.
Management
Observation
Surgical excision for recalcitrant cases

Leiomyoma
Leiomyoma is a benign smooth muscle tumor that presents as a well-defined, painless,
soft-tissue dermal mass. They may present within vascular, dermal, or deep soft tissue.
Most leiomyomas in the hand typically appear to be associated with vascular structures.
This slow-growing mass occasionally may become painful if calcification develops as part
of its vascular variant. Plain radiographs may be helpful in this scenario. MRI will reveal a
well-circumscribed round or oval mass that is hyperintense to muscle on T1-weighted

Granular Cell Tumor
Etiology
Currently thought to originate from neural tissue
Most commonly middle-aged African-American women
Diagnosis
Small, poorly defined nodule in subcutaneous tissue
Biopsy


Granular Cell Tumor
Granular cell tumors are relatively uncommon benign tumors that may present in the
hand. Although a subject of debate, many believe this tumor originates from neural
tissue. The incidence is reportedly higher in African Americans and women. The mass
typically is slow-growing and asymptomatic. The mass may feel mobile if present
subcutaneously and fixed if deep. Histologically, they appear as sheets of elongated cells.
If necessary, excision typically is curative. Recurrences are rare.1

Ganglions/Mucous Cysts/Retinacular Cysts
Etiology
Most common hand and wrist soft-tissue mass
Possibly mucoid degeneration of collagen tissue
Commonly at wrist, flexor sheath (retinacular cyst), and DIP joint (mucoid cyst)
Associated with osteoarthritis
Dorsal wrist cysts originate from scapholunate joint.
Volar wrist ganglia often originate from radioscaphoid or scaphotrapezial joints.
Filled with synovial fluid
Diagnosis
Smooth or lobulated
One of the only masses that can decrease in size (nearly pathognomonic)

Can transilluminate

Despite being one of the most common bumps in the hand and wrist, the precise
etiology and pathogenesis of ganglion cysts remains elusive. Patients who seek care
often do so because of pain; however, most ganglions are not painful. The relationship
of ganglions to pain is limited. Current theory proposes that ganglion cysts develop from
mucoid degeneration of collagen tissue from a joint capsule or synovial sheath. They
develop into a mucin-filled cavity with a wall composed of flattened collagen fibers and
compressed cells but without a true epithelial lining. Their intimate association with a
joint or synovial sheath fluid may result in fluctuation in size.1 In consulting a patient
with a ganglion cyst, surgeons must remember that misconceptions are common.
Patients may fear cancer, pain, or spread of the problem. Gentle correction of these
misconceptions is important before any invasive management; this may take time and
more than one visit or correspondence.9
Ganglion cysts can be accommodated and observed. Some studies report that almost
one-half (42%) of ganglion cysts resolve, meaning they are no longer visible.9 Patients
should understand that the cyst may still be present and may reinflate. Corticosteroid
injection after aspiration appears to offer only potential risks with no potential
advantages. Surgeons should exercise caution with aspiration of volar radial wrist
masses because of the proximity of the radial artery. In general, surgeons may palpate
the radial artery and then apply the needle outside of that region.1,9
Informed patients usually elect to undergo surgical treatment for aesthetic concerns, not
pain. The cyst should be resected at the origin base. The capsule can be left open.
Whether a specimen should be routinely submitted for pathologic analysis in patients
with a classically presenting ganglion cyst is a subject of debate.9 A brief period (1 to 2
weeks) of immobilization may be considered for comfort but is not required. Resect
dorsal osteophytes with a mucoid cyst (DIP joint ganglion) to minimize recurrence. At the
DIP joint, beware of the germinal matrix and terminal extensor tendon.1,9

Gout/Pseudogout
Gout and pseudogout are crystal deposition diseases that result in extracellular fluid
crystal saturation. Gout results in monosodium urate crystal deposition, whereas
pseudogout results from calcium pyrophosphate crystal accumulation.
With accompanying joint involvement, radiographs classically reveal erosion on both
sides of joint surfaces. This finding is not observed in malignant lesions but may be
observed in infection. For most patients with an acute flare of gout or pseudogout, the
initial approach is to consider infection and, if low probability or tests are normal,
manage the inflammatory component of the disease process.10 A brief period of
immobilization, rest, and anti-inflammatory medications often can adequately manage
symptoms as acute inflammation resolves.
In chronic cases with deposition of enlarging tophi, surgical management may be
warranted. Complete resection often is difficult to achieve; however, debulking may be
adequate to reduce symptoms and address skin compromise. In extreme cases with
evidence of necrotic tendon, joint destruction, or ischemic tissue, surgical management

Enchondroma
Enchondromas are benign growths of hyaline cartilage within medullary bone and the
most common primary bone tumor in the hand. They are thought to result from a
portion of endochondral ossification becoming entrapped within the medullary space.
Most of these lesions are asymptomatic; however, some may present after a pathologic
fracture.
Radiographs will reveal a well-defined medullary lesion centrally located with
calcifications. Radiographic and histologic features in the hand may appear more
aggressive than in other parts of the body. Histologically, more cellular atypia may be
deemed acceptable compared with other locations, such as the femur. Currently,

dehydrogenase enzymes.11 Distinguishing an enchondroma from a malignant cartilage
tumor may be difficult in the hand and must be done in close consultation with a
pathologist, taking into account the patient’s history, physical examination, imaging
studies, and histologic features. Asymptomatic enchondromas can be monitored in most
patients. If concerning radiographic features are present, a biopsy can be performed.

Benign Bone Cysts
Unicameral bone cysts are considered the most common bone lesion in the immature
skeleton. Currently, they are thought to result from elevated intraosseous pressure that
leads to necrosis of the local bone and accumulation of protein-rich straw-colored fluid.
Studies report that up to two-thirds of patients present with a pathologic fracture.14 If a
small portion of the cortical wall breaks off and becomes suspended within the cavity of
the lesion, the classic fallen leaf sign is observed.
These lesions typically are painless unless a pathologic fracture occurs. Unicameral bone
cysts may not necessarily heal after fracture. With recurrence of pathologic fractures or
persistent pain, aspiration, injection, or curettage/bone grafting can be
recommended.2,14 ABCs are similar in presentation to unicameral bone cysts and also
may present after pathologic fracture. They also occur in younger patients (in their
teenage years or twenties).
Surgeons should remember that ABCs can occur as a secondary lesion within another
bone lesion, such as giant cell tumor, fibrous dysplasia, or chondroblastoma, in
approximately 30% of patients. Currently, ABCs are thought to result from an induction

Squamous Cell Carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is considered the most common skin tumor encountered
in the hand. It results from uncontrolled proliferation of epidermal keratinocytes and is
intimately associated with solar skin damage. The precursor of SCC typically is actinic
keratosis. Studies report that 6% to 10% of actinic keratosis lesions progress into SCC.15
Actinic keratosis appears as smaller than 1-cm scaling or keratotic papules on the
dorsum of the hand in elderly patients with fair skin. SCCs appear similarly but are larger
and more indurated, with propensity for ulceration and bleeding. Dissimilar from actinic
keratosis, SCC typically appears singly.2
Because SCCs are associated with a risk for metastasis, all suspicious lesions should be
biopsied. High-risk features of SCC are greater than 2 cm in size at presentation, a depth
greater than 2 mm, location on hair-bearing area, perineural invasion, and poor
histologic differentiation.15 SCC in situ (Bowen disease) may be managed nonsurgically
via cryotherapy, electrodissection and curettage, photodynamic therapy, or radiation
therapy.
Surgical management is indicated for low-risk or high-risk SCC. With traditional surgical
excision, surgeons should achieve 4-mm margins for low-risk lesions and 6-mm margins
for high-risk lesions.2,15 Currently, Mohs surgery (ie, same-sitting incremental excisions)
is the recommended approach for high-risk lesions because it may lead to a low
recurrence rate and is tissue-sparing.15

Chondrosarcoma
Chondrosarcoma is the most common malignant bone tumor encountered in the hand.
It is considered to be a diverse group of tumors with a wide range of presentation and
prognosis. Chondrosarcoma results from the proliferation of malignant cells that
resemble chondrocytes. These malignant cells originate in the medullary space and can
produce hyaline, myxoid, or fibromyxoid cartilage.17
Chondrosarcoma typically presents in patients aged 20 to 70 years and is uncommon in
pediatric patients. Dissimilar from most other types of malignant tumors of bone, most
patients with chondrosarcoma in the hand present with an insidious protracted course
of pain, mild swelling, and progressive difficulty with activities. Initial workup will involve
plain radiographs followed by MRI or CT. Imaging studies will reveal a lytic lesion with
punctate or popcorn calcifications and endosteal scalloping. CT scans of the chest are
used to determine if a patient has pulmonary metastasis.8,17
Distinguishing between low-grade chondrosarcoma from an enchondroma remains
difficult, particularly in the hand. A thorough patient history remains critically important
because enchondromas typically result in minimal to no pain and often are found
incidentally. Distinguishing between low-grade (grade I) and higher-grade (grade II and
grade III) is important because management and prognosis substantially differ. Evidence
of periosteal reaction, substantial cortical changes, or extraosseous tumor is attributed
to grade II or grade III chondrosarcomas. Similarly, histologic changes of loss or scarce
resemblance of normal-appearing cartilage typically is associated with higher grade
chondrosarcomas. Conversely, enchondromas may appear more aggressive and similar
to low-grade chondrosarcomas. Close consultation with a pathologist and consideration
of the entire clinical picture are critical.8,17

Osteosarcoma
In the United States, osteosarcoma is the second most common primary bone
malignancy in children and adolescents, only behind lymphoma.18 It also has a second
peak in incidence in elderly patients as a secondary tumor resulting from prior radiation
therapy or underlying bone disease (Paget).
Patients typically present in a delayed fashion with regional pain and swelling. Currently,
almost all patients are thought to have micro-metastasis at presentation; however, only
25% have definitive radiographic confirmation.18 The most common locations of
metastasis are the lungs and skeletal system. The presence of radiographically evident
metastasis remains the most important prognostic indicator. The recommended work
up of a patient in whom osteosarcoma is suspected should include radiographs and MRI
of the entire bone, CT of the chest, and bone scintigraphy. This should be completed
before a biopsy is performed.
Standard management of osteosarcoma includes multiagent chemotherapy and surgical
resection or amputation. In the United States, the typically recommended chemotherapy
